co_shakespearean_theatre_revolution_butt.blurb: A pair of neighbouring formations on the north rim of the upper canyon at Castlewood Canyon State Park, southeast of Denver. The main wall faces southwest and is streaked with a tall black water stain. Fourteen routes are split evenly between bolted lines and gear climbs, with a lone top rope and a single aid line. Difficulty leans hard: a few climbs sit in the 5.7 to 5.9 range, then most of the rest fall in the 5.11 to 5.12 bracket. The rock is conglomerate. A well-known boulder traverse called The Drain runs between the two formations, so bouldering mixes in with the roped climbing. Expect a descent on foot into the canyon before reaching the base.

co_washout_the.blurb: An erosion-cut gully in Unaweep Canyon near Grand Junction, tucked between the Middle and Upper sections of Mother's Buttress. Most of the fourteen climbs are traditional, with one bolted line, and they were developed with newer leaders in mind. The grade spread starts with scrambling-level ground and low fifth class, with the bulk at 5.8 to 5.9 and just a couple of harder pitches near 5.10 and 5.11. The stone is granite. Loose rock and dusty ledges are possible and rockfall happens, so wear a helmet and keep young children elsewhere. A standard rack with doubled cams and a 60 m rope covers everything.
co_washout_the.approach: From the base trail below Mother's Buttress, turn left and follow it along to the gully that separates the Middle and Upper sections.

co_west_block.blurb: A boulder cluster in the Turtle Lake bouldering area just west of Durango, where the sandstone varies in quality and the problems sit close to the road. Fourteen problems here cover a wide range: several easy ones around V0, a handful in the V2 to V4 band, and a few much harder lines reaching into V8 and V9 territory. Some are tall highballs while others are short, so look closely at landings before committing. It suits a mixed group where beginners can warm up and strong boulderers have real projects.

co_dome_the.blurb: A small south-facing gneiss crag in 10 Mile Canyon beside I-70 near Frisco, at roughly 9,500 feet. Slab, face and roof features give a mix of gear routes and a few bolted lines, mostly gentle in angle with a couple of steeper pitches. Of the fourteen climbs here, the large majority are trad. Grades run from around 5.6 up to 5.11, with most clustering in the 5.7 to 5.8 range. The south exposure bakes the wall in sun, which stretches the season through spring, summer and autumn whenever snow has cleared. Routes are short, up to about 100 feet, and the walk is only a few minutes.
co_dome_the.parking_note: Leave the car in the grassy pullout beside I-70 just west of the Frisco exit; wooden signs on old power-pole stumps mark the spot.

co_roadside_boulder_3.blurb: The boulders nearest the parking pullouts at Turtle Lake, west of Durango, so the walk-in is about as short as bouldering gets. The sandstone is of mixed quality. Fourteen problems here run mostly from V2 to V4, with V3 the most common, plus one V1 warm-up and a single hard line around V6. Several are sit starts, and at least one finishes with a dyno. It makes a good quick session close to town for climbers working the middle grades.

co_lookout_mountain_crag.blurb: A compact gneiss wall about 65 feet high, just above Golden on Lookout Mountain Road. It packs a mix of crack, dihedral, face and arete lines, including a roof partway up one face. Half of the fourteen climbs are traditional, with a handful of top ropes, two bolted lines and one aid route. Grades start near 5.6 and mostly sit between 5.7 and 5.9, with a few at 5.10 and one 5.11. The approach is a couple of minutes on a dirt path, and the descent to the base is loose. Rattlesnakes live in the dry scrub, and warm days are best saved for morning or late afternoon.
co_lookout_mountain_crag.parking_note: Pullouts along Lookout Mountain Road, a short drive up from Golden, serve the crag; a brief trail leads from the first one.
